rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed to seek a faster fully resolved method, using the substantial resolution margin.
The 6-minute gradient retains maximum CRF with a minimum resolution of 2.46. Shorten by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be maintained at a lower analysis time.

The 4-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF but leaves only a small resolution margin for the earliest pair. Raise temperature by one step to test faster elution and temperature-dependent selectivity while retaining the fully resolved 40 C method as the fallback.

Heating weakened the critical early-pair separation, so test whether cooling to 25 C provides enough selectivity to support the shortest available gradient. Keep the fully resolved 4-minute, 40 C method as the fallback.

Reduce the gradient slope at 25 C to improve the early pair from R = 1.23 toward full resolution while retaining a 2-minute gradient. The final hold at 75% organic will test whether the last compound still elutes faster than in the fully resolved 4-minute method.

Increase the endpoint by one grid step to accelerate the late peak during the final hold. This tests whether the early pair can retain R ≥ 1.5 despite the slightly steeper gradient, with injection 6 providing the fully resolved fallback.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce the gradient slope while preserving the stronger final hold. This may recover the small early-pair resolution deficit in injection 7 and retain its faster late-peak elution.

Shift both endpoints upward one grid step, preserving the slope that gave full resolution in injection 8. The stronger final hold should accelerate the last peak, while testing whether the early-pair resolution survives the higher starting organic fraction.

Shift both endpoints upward another grid step while retaining the successful gradient slope and temperature. This should shorten late-peak retention further, with the early pair monitored for loss of resolution at the higher starting organic fraction.

Shift the gradient window upward one more step to the maximum endpoint, preserving the slope that has maintained full resolution. This should further accelerate the last peak while testing the early pair at a higher starting organic fraction.

Raise only the starting organic fraction one step to narrow the gradient window and seek earlier final elution. The shallower slope may improve separation, but the earliest pair must be checked for compression toward the dead time.

Use the improved early-pair resolution margin to test a 5 C temperature increase for faster final elution. Keep the endpoints fixed to isolate the temperature effect, with injection 12 as the fully resolved fallback.

Narrow the gradient window by raising the starting organic fraction one step to seek faster elution without further heating. This tests whether the shallower slope preserves early-pair resolution or whether elution near the dead time becomes limiting.

Return to the starting fraction that preserved early-pair separation and test one additional temperature step for faster elution. This brackets the heating limit around injection 13, the fastest fully resolved method so far.

Injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved method; further heating or increasing the starting fraction compromised the early pair. Lower the endpoint one step to test whether a modest increase in late-peak retention buys a useful resolution margin while preserving maximum CRF.

Shift injection 13's gradient window down one step while preserving its slope and temperature to test a fast alternative with the early peaks farther from the dead time. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated method at the maximum CRF.

Cool injection 16 by one step to strengthen the limiting early-pair separation while keeping a short gradient and strong final hold. This tests a potentially more robust maximum-CRF alternative to injection 13, which remains the fastest fully resolved method.

Shift injection 18's window down one step at the same slope to move the early peaks away from the dead time and test a larger separation margin. Maximum CRF is already achieved; injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved option.

Test the remaining nearby high-endpoint method to determine whether moving the early peaks away from the dead time preserves full resolution at 30 C. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method; this run completes its local starting-fraction comparison.

Back off the endpoint from injection 11 by one step to seek greater early-pair resolution while keeping the last peak near 3 minutes. This refines a fast maximum-CRF alternative; injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved method demonstrated.

Test whether cooling restores the early-pair resolution lost at this starting fraction in injection 14, completing the nearby high-organic boundary check. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method at the maximum CRF of 1.000.

Back off to the starting fraction that preserves early-pair separation and lower the endpoint to test a larger resolution margin with a short final hold. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method; this run refines a less marginal alternative.

Raise injection 23's temperature one step to shorten late-peak retention while testing whether its early-pair resolution margin preserves maximum CRF. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Test a final nearby alternative expected to retain full resolution while moving the earliest peaks farther from the dead time. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
